changes.before: Complete first_items(items, limit). Return a list containing at most the first limit items from an iterable. limit is a nonnegative integer. Do not consume more items than needed. The iterable may be finite or endless; never convert the entire input to a list first.
changes.after: Take a small preview without reading all the items.

before: An iterable can supply values one at a time. An iterator remembers where it has reached; iter(items) creates an iterator from an iterable, and next(iterator) obtains its next value.
itertools.islice takes a limited portion without first collecting every value. from itertools import islice imports it.

```python
from itertools import islice
stream = iter(["A", "B", "C"])
preview = list(islice(stream, 2))
print(preview)
print(next(stream))
```
The preview is ["A", "B"]. The next stream value is "C" because the first two have already been consumed.
list collects the selected finite portion into a list. Put islice inside list, not list around the unlimited original stream.
islice(items, limit) stops after at most limit values. A shorter input returns what is available; a zero limit selects nothing.
An iterator is not automatically restarted after a preview. Reusing it continues from its current position. A fresh iterator is a different object.
The exercise accepts only nonnegative integer limits. Handling arbitrary invalid limits is a different contract, not required here.
after: An iterable is something you can take values from one at a time. An iterator remembers where it has reached. `iter(items)` makes an iterator. `next(iterator)` gets its next value.
`itertools.islice` takes only a limited part without first collecting every value. The line `from itertools import islice` makes `islice` available to use.

Look at how a preview moves the same iterator:
```python
from itertools import islice
stream = iter(["A", "B", "C"])
preview = list(islice(stream, 2))
print(preview)
print(next(stream))
```
The preview is `["A", "B"]`. The next stream value is `"C"` because the first two have already been consumed.
`list` turns the chosen part into a list. Put `islice` inside `list`, like `list(islice(items, limit))`. Do not wrap the whole stream in `list` first.

`islice(items, limit)` stops after at most `limit` values. If the input is shorter, it returns what is available. A `limit` of zero selects nothing. This also works for an endless input because it stops at the limit.

An iterator does not restart after a preview. Using the same iterator again continues from where it stopped.

Making another iterator from a reusable list gives a separate position. Calling `iter` on an existing iterator normally gives that same iterator, so it does not reset it.
The exercise accepts only nonnegative integer limits: whole numbers zero or more. Handling other limits is a different job, not required here.
